items.log_text: Inkle loom pegged to the bunk post. Warped with nettle two-ply in alternating sheds. Twenty-two centimetres wide, pattern plain. First band off the loom — rough at the selvedge but the body is even. Will do for belt strapping.
Hemp singles warp — narrower sett this time. Picked a two-over-two float in the heddle shed. It shows as a faint ridge. Durable enough for shoulder-strap load if doubled back on itself at the buckle.

Wall-mounted frame allows a longer warp. Linen two-ply at thirty ends per centimetre is the finest we have managed. Selvedge nearly straight for the last metre. Cut into two strips — one for Lara's boot facing, one stored flat.
Mixed warp — nettle in the raised shed, hemp in the lowered. The two-colour stripe is unintentional but makes the bands easier to identify when sorting supplies. Will repeat.

Backstrap loom uses the shelter wall as the fixed warp post. Body tension controls the shed. Forty centimetres wide — wider than the inkle and harder to beat evenly. Hemp two-ply holds tension well. Weft passes are uneven at the edges but consistent in the centre.

Singles warp on the backstrap — risky, but the warp threads survived. Nettle singles break at sharp bends; kept the shed stick narrow and the angle shallow. Cloth came off loose. Will soak-shrink before cutting.

Rigid heddle cut from salvage comb teeth. Slots rough but functional. Linen two-ply warp beats down cleanly at twenty-two picks per centimetre. Cloth is dense enough for a water-bag lining if waxed afterwards.

Dog fur two-ply warp — softer hand than any plant fibre we have. Sheds cleanly. Weft is hemp singles beaten very open. The resulting fabric is a loose scrim, lightweight and warm. First true insulating cloth we have made.
